title: Priority 1: Getting a View and Setting a Vision Across Systems
author: Michael B. Horn, Angela Jackson, Mallory Dwinal-Palisch and Danny Curtis
summary: This is the second paper in a six-part state policy playbook from the Clayton Christensen Institute on building integrated education-to-career systems, republished on Michael Horn's Substack. It argues that K-12, higher education and workforce agencies cannot each improve in isolation, so a state's first priority is a coherent cross-system strategy rather than any single programmatic reform. Three recommendations follow: set an effective vision that describes outcomes without prescribing solutions, build a cross-agency governance body with real authority and a single accountable leader, and inform strategy with shared longitudinal data systems. Each is illustrated with a state example (Texas Tri-Agency charges, Arkansas Governor's Workforce Cabinet, Maryland Longitudinal Data System) and paired with a Chesterton's Fence caution about what fragmentation protects. The paper is distinctive for insisting on coordination without consolidating the distinct missions of schools, colleges and training providers.
points: An effective statewide vision names the outcomes learners and providers should reach while leaving agencies room to design the reforms, avoiding both vagueness and over-prescription.
Texas learned that charges focused on activities produced parallel agency work, and only a learner-centered vision with outcomes no agency could deliver alone created real collaboration.
Cross-agency governance works when it reports to the governor, includes department heads, and puts one named leader (Arkansas's Chief Workforce Officer) in charge of follow-through.
Shared data systems such as Maryland's MLDS let states see how learners move between K-12, college and work, but they depend on trust built through governance before access expands.
Each recommendation carries a Chesterton's Fence check: the goal is coordination, not consolidation, so the distinct missions and safeguards of each system are preserved.
quotes: A vision is not a plan or even a strategy. It is the North Star that sets the direction for those documents and makes them coherent.

At their best, state governments should build something more akin to a GPS. A statewide vision establishes a shared destination. A coordinated statewide strategy charts the path to that destination for policymakers and providers alike.

A useful vision must strike the right balance between the two. It should provide enough specificity to guide action, while leaving enough room for the people closest to these systems to shape strategy and implementation.

Without a clearer picture of what the agencies were trying to accomplish together, they had less reason to develop a shared understanding of the state’s talent pipeline or coordinate their work around it.
Another important feature of the Cabinet is the Chief Workforce Officer role. Cross-agency bodies often falter when coordination is everyone’s responsibility and no one’s job.
The goal is coordination, not consolidation. A cross-agency body should improve collaboration while preserving the distinct missions, safeguards, and expertise of each system.

State leaders cannot effectively manage what they cannot measure. When K–12, higher education, and workforce data are siloed, policymakers can measure what is happening within each segment of the pipeline, but not how learners move between them.
The goal, then, is governed data sharing: linking information where there is a clear public purpose, a defined user need, and a strong legal and ethical basis for access.
